entities.name: California State University, Los Angeles
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
California State University, Los Angeles (Cal State LA, CSULA, founded 1947) is a public university in Los Angeles, California, part of the California State University system — serving one of America's most ethnically diverse urban student populations, with approximately 70% of students from minority backgrounds and a majority Hispanic-serving institution designation, making it one of the most diverse major universities in the United States and a critical institution of educational opportunity in one of the world's largest and most diverse urban centers.

Cal State LA's founding in 1947 — two years before CSULB — responded to the same post-WWII Southern California population surge, but with a focus on Los Angeles's urban core. The university's East Los Angeles location situates it in the heart of the city's largest Latino community, and its enrollment patterns reflect this geography: Cal State LA has been a Hispanic-Serving Institution (HSI) since the designation was created, with its student body majority Hispanic and serving large proportions of first-generation college students.

Cal State LA has achieved significant recognition for its educational access mission: consistently ranked among America's top universities for social mobility, it graduates large numbers of first-generation college students from working-class backgrounds into professional careers. The university's research programs (including CSULA's NASA-affiliated Jet Propulsion Laboratory collaborations) combine with its access mission, and its College of Engineering, Computer Science, and Technology has produced graduates who have contributed significantly to Los Angeles's technology and aerospace industries.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: California State University Los Angeles — a top-ranked Hispanic-Serving Institution in America's largest Latino urban community, consistently recognized for exceptional social mobility — is historically significant as a model of urban educational access for America's most diverse city.
